introduction-the-works-on-my-machine-cri.core: Developers describe workloads in docker-compose locally, Helm for staging and something else for production, so configuration drifts between environments. Score is a platform-agnostic workload spec written once and translated to each target.

first_principles.problem: An app works in docker-compose but fails in Kubernetes because the env vars, ports and dependencies were described differently.
truths: Several formats describe the same workload.
Developers care about intent, not platform specifics.
derivation: **Generate** platform files (Compose, Helm/K8s) with Score implementations.

analogy.title: Writing a recipe once for any kitchen
analogy.story: The same recipe works on a gas stove or an induction hob; the cook translates it to the equipment.
analogy.breaks: Score covers common workload needs; exotic platform features need extensions.

example.title: Compose vs Helm drift
example.outcome: one source of truth for workload intent.

check.a: Configuration drift from describing the same workload differently for each environment and platform.

the-architecture-the-sheet-music-analogy.core: Score works like sheet music. The composer (developer) writes the score (workload spec), and different orchestras (platforms like Docker Compose or Kubernetes) perform it with their own instruments (implementations), each interpreting the same music faithfully.

first_principles.problem: Developers must learn every platform's dialect to describe the same application.
truths: Intent can be separated from execution.

analogy.title: Sheet music performed by different orchestras
analogy.story: The same score sounds right whether played by a chamber group or a full orchestra.
analogy.breaks: Implementations can differ in fidelity, so test the outputs.

example.title: One spec, two outputs
flow: score-compose → compose file with a postgres container
score-k8s → Deployment + claim for managed DB

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: The same intent, appropriate per environment.

example.outcome: developer intent separated from platform execution.

check.q: In the Score analogy, what plays the role of the orchestra?
check.a: The target platform and its Score implementation (e.g. score-compose or score-k8s).

anatomy-of-a-scoreyaml.core: A score.yaml has apiVersion and metadata (name), containers (image, command, variables, files), resources (dependencies like databases, DNS and routes, by type) and service (ports). Variables can reference resource outputs with ${resources.db.host}.

first_principles.problem: Developers need a clear, minimal format to express what their workload needs.
truths: Workloads need containers, dependencies and exposure.
Dependencies should be declared, not hard-coded.

analogy.title: A party invitation with RSVP needs
analogy.story: 'Bring yourself (container), we need a venue and catering (resources), arrive at door 8080 (service).'
analogy.breaks: Score's resource types depend on what the platform implementation supports.

example.title: A complete score.yaml
example.outcome: you can read and write score.yaml.

check.q: How does a container in score.yaml get a database's connection details?
check.a: Through variable references to resource outputs, like ${resources.db.host}.

environment-agnostic-context-injection.core: Score keeps environment-specific values out of the spec. Containers reference abstract resource outputs, and each environment's implementation injects the real values (a local container DB vs a managed RDS endpoint, dev vs prod secrets) at generation or deploy time.

first_principles.problem: Hard-coded hosts and environment-specific config in deployment files mean separate files per environment, and drift.
truths: The same workload runs in different contexts.
derivation: Reference **${resources.*}** and **${metadata.*}** rather than literal values.
The platform **provisions or binds** resources per environment.

analogy.title: A form letter with mail-merge fields
analogy.story: 'Dear {name}' is filled in differently for each recipient while the letter stays the same.
analogy.breaks: Some environment differences (scale, feature flags) still need platform-level overrides.

check.q: How does Score keep specs environment-agnostic?
check.a: Containers reference abstract resource outputs, which each environment's platform resolves to real values.

score-in-a-platform-engineering-workflow.core: Score sits above Kubernetes, Helm, Terraform and Compose rather than replacing them. Developers own score.yaml, while platform teams own implementations and resource provisioners, often orchestrated by a platform orchestrator (like Humanitec) or CI that generates manifests for GitOps.

first_principles.problem: Teams don't see where a workload spec fits among the existing tools.
truths: Generated manifests can flow into GitOps.
derivation: **CI** runs score-k8s/score-compose (or an orchestrator) to generate manifests.

analogy.title: An architect, builder and city services
analogy.story: The architect draws the plans, the builder constructs to local codes and the utilities hook up power and water.
analogy.breaks: It's another layer to learn and maintain, so it's worth it at scale or across many environments.

example.title: An end-to-end flow
flow: CI: score-k8s generate → manifests + Redis claim
Argo CD syncs; Crossplane provisions Redis

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: A developer adds a dependency without touching infra code.

example.outcome: clean separation of developer and platform concerns.

check.q: Does Score replace Kubernetes or Helm?
check.a: No. It sits above them, generating platform-native configuration from a workload spec.
